provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate held at 7.6% in March 20261, the highest of the four largest provinces, while the employment rate slipped 0.1 percentage points to 59.6% and participation stayed at 64.6%1. The cross-reference engine links the current rate to 136 Ontario projects ($9.59B) in employment-sensitive sectors — healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, and residential2.

Headline CPI stood at -1.1% year-over-year in February 2026, from -1.6% in January3 — the only negative headline rate posted by any province this month. The dossier attributes the negative reading to the HST base-year effect from the 2025 federal GST holiday. Housing starts rose 2.3% month-over-month to 67,274 units (SAAR) in February4, from 65,757 the prior month. Real GDP growth is recorded at +1.2% for 2024 in the provincial accounts5.

Ontario Budget 2026, tabled March 26, set a $244.2 billion spending envelope and projected a $13.8 billion deficit for 2026-276. The budget's 10-year capital plan totals $210 billion, including $37 billion in 2026-277. The project database tracks 546 Ontario projects ($253.0B total parsed value), led by infrastructure with 199 projects ($150.2B); the top pipeline entries are Highway 413 and Bradford Bypass ($31.0B, Under Construction), the Ontario Line ($27.4B, Under Construction), and GO Expansion ($26.1B, Under Construction)2. 26 Ontario projects sit in the federal Impact Assessment Registry — the largest provincial share — including the New Nuclear at Wesleyville Project and the CAFTA Winona Range upgrades8.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec recorded the largest monthly unemployment decline of the four largest provinces in March 2026, with the rate falling 0.5 percentage points to 5.4% — the lowest big-province reading1. The employment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 60.9%, while participation edged down 0.1 percentage points to 64.4%1. The cross-reference engine links the new rate to 208 Quebec projects in employment-sensitive sectors2.

Headline CPI slipped to +0.6% year-over-year in February 2026, from +0.7% in January3. Housing starts rose 2.8% month-over-month to 53,461 units (SAAR) in February4. Provincial real GDP growth was +1.3% in 20245. Quebec international exports were $89.0 billion and imports $99.9 billion in December 20256.

The 2026-27 Quebec Budget, released March 25, tabled an $8.6 billion deficit for 2026-27 and added $5 billion to the 10-year capital plan, bringing it to $167 billion7. The budget allocated $1.7 billion over five years for economic transformation, including $480 million for critical and strategic minerals. The project database tracks 448 Quebec projects ($87.8B), with the power and energy sector holding 29 projects ($35.4B) — led by the Parc éolien zone Chamouchouane ($9.0B, Proposed) and a green hydrogen production plant ($4.0B, Under Review)2. 13 Quebec projects are listed in the federal Impact Assessment Registry, including the Leamy Creek Pathway Re-Naturalization in Gatineau8.

provinces.name: Alberta

Alberta's unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 6.5% in March 20261. The participation rate increased 0.2 percentage points to 68.9% — the highest in Canada — and the employment rate held at 64.4%1. The cross-reference engine links the current unemployment rate to 236 Alberta projects ($107.24B) in employment-sensitive sectors (healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, residential)2.

Headline CPI decelerated 1.5 percentage points to +3.4% year-over-year in February 2026, from +4.9% in January3 — the largest monthly deceleration among the provinces. Housing starts were 48,438 units (SAAR) in February, down 0.9% from 48,896 the prior month4. Provincial real GDP growth stood at +2.7% in 20245.

Alberta Budget 2026, released February 27, introduced an 8% bracket on the first $60,000 of taxable income and tabled a $28.3 billion three-year capital plan6. The project database tracks 686 Alberta projects ($349.5B), with the power/energy sector holding 124 projects ($137.3B) as the largest sector by value2. The Alberta oil, gas, and power/energy pipeline combined totals 188 projects ($198.3B), led by the Pathways Alliance Carbon Capture and Storage Hub Phase 1 ($16.5B, Proposed) and AOSP Jackpine ($12.0B, Approved)2. 24 Alberta projects sit in the federal Impact Assessment Registry — second only to Ontario — including new Under Review entries for Tsuut'ina Bullhead Road Sewer Line and Mînî Thnî Lift Station7.

provinces.name: Yukon
provinces.analysis:
Yukon's unemployment rate stood at 3.9% in the February 2026 LFS — the lowest of the three territories1. Territorial LFS data is released with a lag compared with provincial series, so the March 2026 reading is not yet published. The cross-reference engine links the rate to 15 Yukon projects ($0.51B) in employment-sensitive sectors2.

Real GDP contracted 3.3% in 2024 in the provincial and territorial accounts, driven by declines in placer gold and mineral-extraction output3. Territorial monthly CPI is not published by Statistics Canada; Yukon monthly CPI is reported only at the Whitehorse city level as a separate release, which is the closest proxy available4. Housing starts and participation rates are not in the published provincial indicator series for the territory for this period.

The project database tracks 115 Yukon projects ($47.3B total parsed value) — a pipeline dominated by the Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment at $40.0 billion (Proposed), which places defence as the largest sector by value with 1 project ($40.0B)2. Top non-defence entries are Casino Mine ($3.62B, Proposed), the Whitehorse Power Centres Project ($520M, Proposed), Kudz Ze Kayah zinc/copper ($489M, Under Review), and the Yukon Budget 2026 Capital Plan ($385M, Proposed)5. Yukon records 0 federal Impact Assessment Registry entries this week; Yukon projects are assessed under the Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Act rather than the federal Impact Assessment Act6.

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate stood at 10.8% in the February 2026 LFS — the highest rate in Canada1. Territorial LFS data is released with a lag; the March 2026 reading has not yet been published. The cross-reference engine links the rate to 10 Nunavut projects ($1.41B) in employment-sensitive sectors2.

Real GDP expanded 7.5% in 2024 in the provincial and territorial accounts — the fastest growth rate in Canada — driven by mining output3. Territorial monthly CPI is not published by Statistics Canada; Nunavut monthly CPI is reported only at the Iqaluit city level, which is the closest proxy available4. Housing starts and participation rates are not in the published indicator series for the territory for this period.

The project database tracks 55 Nunavut projects ($38.9B total parsed value), with defence as the largest sector by value at 1 project ($32.0B) — the Northern Defence and Infrastructure Nunavut Military Basing Package (Proposed)2. Top non-defence entries are Baffinland Mary River Steensby Rail and Port Expansion ($3.0B, Approved), the Back River Gold Project ($610M, Under Construction), and the Nunavut 750 Homes Initiative ($480M, Under Construction) — of which the first 10 homes have been delivered to Baker Lake under the federal-territorial housing agreement5. Infrastructure accounts for 19 projects and tourism/culture for 62. Nunavut records 0 federal Impact Assessment Registry entries this week; the territory uses the Nunavut Impact Review Board process under the Nunavut Agreement6.

projects.name: Northern Defence and Infrastructure — Nunavut Military Bases
projects.description: Prime Minister Carney announced $32B for northern defence and infrastructure, including new forward operating locations in Iqaluit and Northern Operation Support Nodes in Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet. Facilities include upgraded airfields, hangars, ammunition compounds, fuel facilities, and housing over approximately 10 years.

projects.name: Baffinland Mary River Steensby Rail and Port Expansion
projects.description: Baffinland Iron Mines completed Inuit consultation for the Steensby Component of the Mary River project, clearing the final requirement to advance into construction. The expansion includes a railway and deepwater port at Steensby Inlet, increasing production from 4.2 to 22 million tonnes per annum. Construction estimated at ~$3B with 2,250 peak construction jobs.

projects.name: Nunavut 750 Homes Initiative
projects.description: The Government of Canada ($250M), Government of Nunavut ($230M), and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated signed an Agreement in Principle to deliver up to 750 homes across the territory. Baker Lake has received 10 of the 750 homes. Up to 30% will use modular/off-site construction methods.

projects.name: Baker Lake Modular Housing — 750-Home Program First Delivery
projects.description: Baker Lake received 10 modular homes built by Ottawa manufacturer Caivan, the first units delivered under the Government of Canada/Nunavut/NTI agreement to build up to 750 homes territory-wide. Build Canada Homes providing up to $250M and Nunavut contributing up to $230M.
